text: Lyndon Baines Johnson (/ˈlɪndən ˈbeɪnz/; August 27, 1908 – January 22, 1973), also known as LBJ, was the 36th president of the United States, serving from 1963 to 1969. He became president after the assassination of John F. Kennedy, under whom he had served as the 37th vice president from 1961 to 1963. A Southern Democrat, Johnson previously represented Texas in Congress for over 23 years, first as a U.S. representative from 1937 to 1949, and then as a U.S. senator from 1949 to 1961. Born in Stonewall, Texas, Johnson worked as a teacher and a congressional aide before winning election to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1937. In 1948, he was controversially declared the winner in the Democratic primary for the U.S. Senate election in Texas before winning the general election. He became Senate majority whip in 1951, Senate Democratic leader in 1953, and majority leader in 1954. Senator Kennedy bested Johnson and his other rivals for the 1960 Democratic presidential nomination before surprising many by offering to make Johnson his vice presidential running mate. The Kennedy–Johnson ticket won the general election. Vice President Johnson assumed the presidency in 1963, after President Kennedy was assassinated. The following year, Johnson won reelection to the presidency in a landslide, winning the largest share of the popular vote for the Democratic Party in history, and the highest for any candidate since the advent of widespread popular elections in the 1820s. Johnson's domestic policy agenda known as the Great Society was aimed at expanding civil rights, public broadcasting, access to health care, aid to education and the arts, urban and rural development, consumer protection, environmentalism, and public services. He sought to create better living conditions for low-income Americans by spearheading the war on poverty. As part of these efforts, Johnson signed the Social Security Amendments of 1965, which resulted in the creation of Medicare and Medicaid. Johnson made the Apollo program a national priority; enacted the Higher Education Act of 1965 which established federally insured student loans; and signed the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 which laid the groundwork for U.S. immigration policy today. Johnson's civil rights legacy was shaped by the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and the Civil Rights Act of 1968. Due to his domestic agenda, Johnson's presidency marked the peak of modern American liberalism in the 20th century. Johnson's foreign policy prioritized containment of communism, including in the ongoing Vietnam War. Johnson began his presidency with near-universal support, but his approval declined throughout his presidency as the public became frustrated with both the Vietnam War and domestic unrest, including race riots, increasing public skepticism with his reports and policies (coined the credibility gap), and increasing crime. Johnson initially sought to run for re-election in 1968; however, following disappointing results in the New Hampshire primary, he withdrew his candidacy. Johnson retired to his Texas ranch and kept a low public profile until he died in 1973. Public opinion and academic assessments of Johnson's legacy have fluctuated greatly. Historians and scholars rank Johnson in the upper tier for his accomplishments regarding domestic policy. His administration passed many major laws that made substantial changes in civil rights, health care, welfare, and education. Conversely, Johnson is heavily criticized for his foreign policy, namely escalating American involvement in the Vietnam War. Lyndon Baines Johnson was born on August 27, 1908, near Stonewall, Texas, in a small farmhouse on the Pedernales River. He was the eldest of five children born to Samuel Ealy Johnson Jr. and Rebekah Baines. Johnson was not given a name until he was three months old, as his parents could not agree on a name that both liked. Finally, he was named after "criminal lawyer—a county lawyer" W. C. Linden, who his father liked; his mother agreed on the condition of spelling it as Lyndon. Johnson had one brother, Sam Houston Johnson, and three sisters, Rebekah, Josefa, and Lucia. Through his mother, he was a great-grandson of Baptist clergyman George Washington Baines. Johnson's paternal grandfather, Samuel Ealy Johnson Sr., was raised Baptist and for a time was a member of the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ). In his later years, Samuel Sr. became a Christadelphian; Samuel Jr. also joined the Christadelphian Church toward the end of his life. Johnson was influenced in his positive attitude toward Jews by the religious beliefs that his family, especially his grandfather, had shared with him. Johnson grew up poor, with his father losing a great deal of money. Biographer Robert Caro described him as being raised "in a land without electricity, where the soil was so rocky that it was hard to earn a living from it." In school, Johnson was a talkative youth who was elected president of his 11th-grade class. He graduated in 1924 from Johnson City High School, where he participated in public speaking, debate, and baseball. At 15, Johnson was the youngest in his class. Pressured by his parents to attend college, he enrolled at a "sub college" of Southwest Texas State Teachers College (SWTSTC) in the summer of 1924, where students from unaccredited high schools could take the 12th-grade courses needed for admission to college. He left the school just weeks after his arrival and decided to move to California. He worked at his cousin's legal practice and in odd jobs before returning to Texas, where he worked as a day laborer. In 1926, Johnson enrolled at SWTSTC. He worked his way through school, participated in debate and campus politics, and edited the school newspaper, The College Star. The college years refined his skills of persuasion and political organization. For nine months, from 1928 to 1929, Johnson paused his studies to teach Mexican–American children at the segregated Welhausen School in Cotulla, Texas, 90 miles (140 km) south of San Antonio. The job helped him to save money to complete his education, and he graduated in 1930 with a Bachelor of Science in history and his certificate of qualification as a high school teacher. He briefly taught at Pearsall High School in Pearsall, Texas before taking a position teaching public speaking at Sam Houston High School in Houston. When he returned to San Marcos in 1965, after signing the Higher Education Act of 1965, Johnson reminisced: "I shall never forget the faces of the boys and the girls in that little Welhausen Mexican School, and I remember even yet the pain of realizing and knowing then that college was closed to practically every one of those children because they were too poor. And I think it was then that I made up my mind that this nation could never rest while the door to knowledge remained closed to any American." After Richard M. Kleberg won a 1931 special election to represent Texas in the United States House of Representatives, he appointed Johnson as his legislative secretary. This marked Johnson's formal introduction to politics. Johnson secured the position on the recommendation of his father and that of state senator Welly Hopkins, for whom Johnson had campaigned in 1930. Kleberg had little interest in the day-to-day duties of a Congressman, instead delegating them to Johnson. After Franklin D. Roosevelt won the 1932 U.S. presidential election, Johnson became a lifelong supporter of Roosevelt's New Deal. Johnson was elected speaker of the "Little Congress", a group of Congressional aides, where he cultivated Congressmen, newspapermen, and lobbyists. Johnson's friends soon included aides to President Roosevelt as well as fellow Texans such as vice president John Nance Garner and congressman Sam Rayburn. In 1935, Johnson was hired as Texas state administrator of the National Youth Administration (NYA). The job allowed him to travel around Texas seeking financial sponsors for NYA construction projects. Within six months, 18,000 young Texans were working on roads, parks, schools, and other public buildings. He resigned two years later to run for Congress. A notoriously tough boss, Johnson often demanded long workdays and work on weekends. He was described by friends, fellow politicians, and historians as motivated by lust for power and control. As Caro observes, "Johnson's ambition was uncommon – in the degree to which it was unencumbered by even the slightest excess weight of ideology, of philosophy, of principles, of beliefs." In 1937, after the death of 13-term congressman James P. Buchanan, Johnson successfully campaigned in a special election for Texas's 10th congressional district, which included Austin and the surrounding Texas Hill Country. He ran on a New Deal platform and was effectively aided by his wife. He served as a U.S. Representative from April 10, 1937, to January 3, 1949. President Roosevelt found Johnson to be a political ally and conduit for information, particularly regarding the internal politics of Texas and the machinations of Vice President John Nance Garner and House Speaker Sam Rayburn. As a member of the House Naval Affairs Committee, Johnson helped plan a huge naval air training base at Corpus Christi, Texas. He also helped establish shipbuilding sites at Houston and Orange, Texas; and a Navy Reserve station in Dallas. Johnson successfully sponsored many federal projects for his home district. One was a program that provided cheap electricity for farmers under the new Rural Electrification Administration (REA), and he secured approval to complete the hydroelectric Mansfield Dam on the Colorado River near Austin. He also sponsored projects that gave his Texas district soil conservation, public housing, lower railroad freight rates, and expanded credit for loans to farmers. He steered the projects towards contractors he knew, such as Herman and George Brown, who financed much of Johnson's future career. During this time Johnson maintained a hostile position towards civil rights legislation like almost all other Southern Democrat legislators; voting against anti-lynching legislation, anti-poll tax legislation and the Fair Employment Practice Committee. In April 1941, U.S. Senator Morris Sheppard of Texas died, triggering a special election. Texas law allowed Johnson to run without giving up his House seat. The election had no primaries or runoff, forcing Johnson to compete against multiple Democrats, including Governor W. Lee "Pappy" O'Daniel. Johnson campaigned aggressively, emphasizing his ties to President Roosevelt, and initially appeared to be leading. However, after late returns came in, O'Daniel narrowly won by 1,311 votes. In The Path to Power, Johnson biographer Robert Caro argues that the election results were manipulated in O'Daniel's favor by lobbyists from Texas' alcohol industry. O'Daniel was a staunch prohibitionist, and as Governor, he had proposed a bill preventing the sale of alcohol within ten miles of a military base; Caro notes how business interests feared the passing of this bill, as preparations for World War II had brought thousands of young soldiers into the region. To prevent the passing of this bill, lobbyists sought to elect O'Daniel to the Senate to place the "wet" lieutenant governor Coke Stevenson in the governorship, and hence rigged ballots in East Texas, swinging the election in O'Daniel's favor. Johnson ultimately lost by just 0.23% of the vote. Though defeated, Johnson retained his House seat and political network, including support from South Texas political boss George Berham Parr. When O'Daniel declined to seek re-election in 1948, Johnson prepared for another Senate run, this time carefully managing vote tallies. He would go on to win the 1948 Democratic primary by just 87 votes. Johnson was a member of the U.S. Naval Reserve when Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941. Two days after the attack, he requested an indefinite leave of absence and applied for active duty, making him one of the first members of Congress to volunteer for an active military role. Johnson was first ordered to the Office of the Chief of Naval Operations to assess the production and manpower problems that were slowing the manufacture of ships and planes. In May 1942, he was appointed President Roosevelt's personal representative to the Navy and was sent on a survey mission of the Pacific theater of combat. Stationed in Australia and New Zealand, it was his duty to find the underreported problems facing U.S. troops in the Pacific and report this firsthand information to Roosevelt. On June 9, 1942, Johnson received the Silver Star from General Douglas MacArthur for gallantry in action during an aerial combat mission over hostile positions in New Guinea. Though accounts differ, Johnson's aircraft, a B-26 bomber, reportedly turned back before reaching the target due to mechanical trouble. Johnson's biographer Robert Caro was quoted as saying "I think that the weight of the evidence at this moment is that the plane was attacked by Zeroes and that he was cool under fire," but also "The fact is, LBJ never got within sight of Japanese forces. His combat experience was a myth." Johnson served in the Pacific through July 1942. He was released from his military active duty after President Roosevelt recalled all active duty legislators back to Washington, D.C. In addition to the Silver Star, Johnson received the Asiatic-Pacific Campaign Medal, and the World War II Victory Medal. In 1948, Johnson again ran for the U.S. Senate and won the general election after being declared winner in a highly controversial Democratic Party primary election against the well-known former governor Coke Stevenson. Johnson drew crowds to fairgrounds with his rented Sikorsky S-51 helicopter, dubbed "The Johnson City Windmill." He raised money to flood the state with campaign circulars and won over conservatives by casting doubts on Stevenson's support for the Taft–Hartley Act (curbing union power). Stevenson came in first in the primary but lacked a majority, so a runoff election was held. The runoff vote count, handled by the Democratic State Central Committee, took a week. Johnson was announced the winner by 87 votes out of 988,295, an extremely narrow margin. However, Johnson's victory was based on 200 "patently fraudulent" ballots reported six days after the election from Box 13 in Jim Wells County, in an area dominated by political boss George Parr. The added names were in alphabetical order and written with the same pen and handwriting, at the end of the list of voters. Some on this part of the list insisted that they had not voted that day. Election judge Luis Salas said in 1977 that he had certified 202 fraudulent ballots, 200 for Johnson, and two for Stevenson. Robert Caro made the case in his 1990 book that Johnson had stolen the election in Jim Wells County, and that there were thousands of fraudulent votes in other counties as well, including 10,000 votes switched in San Antonio. The Democratic State Central Committee voted to certify Johnson's nomination by a majority of one (29–28). The state Democratic convention upheld Johnson. Stevenson went to court, eventually taking his case before the U.S. Supreme Court, but with timely help from his friend and future U.S. Supreme Court Justice Abe Fortas, Johnson prevailed on the basis that jurisdiction over naming a nominee rested with the party, not the federal government. Johnson soundly defeated Republican Jack Porter in the general election in November and went to Washington, permanently dubbed "Landslide Lyndon." Johnson, dismissive of his critics, happily adopted the nickname. During his two terms in the Senate, Johnson drifted rightward. He felt he had to tread carefully lest he offend politically powerful conservative oil and gas interests in Texas, and in part to curry favor with the chamber's powerful southern chairmen, most notably Senator Richard Russell, Democrat from Georgia and leader of the Southern Caucus within the conservative coalition that dominated the Senate. With Russell's support, Johnson won election as Democratic whip in 1951, serving in this capacity until 1953. While serving as whip, Johnson increased his ability to persuade people to reach agreement. As a member of the Senate Committee on Interstate and Foreign Commerce, Johnson was chairman of the Senate subcommittee that refused the re-nomination of Leland Olds—who was opposed by Texas oil and gas interests—as chairman of the Federal Power Commission (FPC) on the grounds that he had been sympathetic towards communism. As a member of the FPC, Olds had played a key role in the development of federal regulation of the natural gas industry. President Truman favored federal control of tidelands oil deposits off the Texas coast. Privately, Johnson told friends that he favored federal control, but in public he staunchly defended states' rights. In 1951–52, Johnson helped pass bills granting 47 states control over 3 miles of offshore lands and Texas, 10.5 miles. Truman vetoed the bills, calling them "robbery in broad daylight." Johnson was appointed to the Senate Armed Services Committee, and became increasingly concerned with the country's military preparedness in the Cold War with the Soviet Union. He became chairman of the Senate Preparedness Investigating Subcommittee, and conducted investigations of defense costs and efficiency. After the Korean War began in 1950, he called for more troops and for improved weapons. Biographer Caro wrote that Johnson was obsessed with having all subcommittee reports be unanimous, maneuvering frequently to gain the backing of all the Republicans. He used his political influence in the Senate to receive broadcast licenses from the Federal Communications Commission in his wife's name. In the 1952 elections, Republicans won a majority in both the House and Senate. In January 1953, the Senate convened.

Deposits off the Texas coast were granted control by legislation passed in 1951–52, which gave 47 states control over 3 miles of offshore lands and Texas, 10.5 miles. President Truman vetoed the bills, calling them "robbery in broad daylight." Johnson was appointed to the Senate Armed Services Committee and became increasingly concerned with military preparedness during the Cold War with the Soviet Union. He chaired the Senate Preparedness Investigating Subcommittee and conducted investigations into defense costs and efficiency. After the Korean War began in 1950, he called for more troops and improved weapons. Biographer Caro noted Johnson was obsessed with achieving unanimous subcommittee reports, frequently maneuvering to secure Republican support. He used his political influence to obtain broadcast licenses from the Federal Communications Commission in his wife's name. In the 1952 elections, Republicans gained majorities in both the House and Senate. In January 1953, Johnson was elected Senate Minority Leader, becoming the most junior senator ever to hold the position. He reformed the seniority system so that Democratic senators, including freshmen, received committee assignments based on expertise rather than seniority. In 1954, Johnson was re-elected to the Senate and, with Democrats gaining a majority, became Senate Majority Leader. President Eisenhower found Johnson more cooperative than Senate Republican leader William F. Knowland, particularly on foreign policy, where Johnson offered bipartisan support. Historians Caro and Dallek consider Johnson the most effective Senate majority leader ever. He was exceptionally skilled at gathering information, with one biographer calling him "the greatest intelligence gatherer Washington has ever known," noting he discovered every senator’s positions, philosophies, and voting preferences. Bobby Baker claimed Johnson sent senators on NATO trips to remove them from votes. Central to Johnson’s control was "The Treatment," which could last ten minutes or four hours and occurred at various locations, including the Johnson Ranch swimming pool, offices, or Senate cloakroom. It combined supplication, accusation, cajolery, scorn, tears, and threats, with Johnson moving in close, his face just a millimeter away, eyes and eyebrows shifting rapidly, and pouring out clippings, memos, and statistics. Mimicry, humor, and analogy made it hypnotic, leaving targets stunned and helpless. In 1956 during the Suez Crisis, Johnson tried to prevent the U.S. government from criticizing Israel for its invasion of the Sinai Peninsula. He was alarmed by the Soviet threat implied by the launch of Sputnik 1 and used his influence to ensure passage of the National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958, which established NASA. Johnson helped create the Senate Aeronautical and Space Committee and became its first chairman. During his tenure as Majority Leader, he did not sign the 1956 Southern Manifesto and shepherded the Civil Rights Acts of 1957 and 1960 to passage—the first such bills since Reconstruction-era legislation. To balance Northern liberals and Southern opposition, he removed key enforcement provisions, such as Title III, which allowed the attorney general to initiate civil actions for preventive relief. Being a Southerner was seen as a barrier for a presidential candidate, and by joining the Democrats' Western regional conference in 1959, Johnson distanced himself further from the Southern Caucus. In 1960, Johnson’s Senate success made him a potential Democratic presidential candidate. James H. Rowe urged him to enter the race in early 1959, but Johnson waited, believing Senator John F. Kennedy’s candidacy would create a division exploitable by Democrats. Johnson planned to sit out the primaries and rely on his legislative record, support from Southern Democrats, and favors owed to him and to Speaker Sam Rayburn. In July 1960, Johnson entered the campaign. His late entry and reluctance to leave Washington allowed Kennedy to gain early support from Democratic state party officials. Johnson underestimated Kennedy’s charm and intelligence compared to his perceived crude "Landslide Lyndon" style. Caro suggests Johnson hesitated due to fear of losing. He attempted to capitalize on Kennedy’s youth, poor health, and lack of a stance on McCarthyism, forming a "Stop Kennedy" coalition with Adlai Stevenson, Stuart Symington, and Hubert Humphrey, which failed. Despite having support from established Democrats and party leaders, Johnson lacked popular approval. At the 1960 Democratic convention, he received 409 votes to Kennedy’s 806 on the only ballot, and the convention nominated Kennedy. Tip O'Neill, a Massachusetts representative, recalled Johnson approached him and said, "Tip, I know you have to support Kennedy at the start, but I'd like to have you with me on the second ballot." O'Neill replied, "Senator, there's not going to be any second ballot." After discussions with party leaders, Kennedy offered Johnson the vice presidential nomination at the Los Angeles Biltmore Hotel on July 14, the morning after Kennedy’s nomination, and Johnson accepted. Whether convention chairman LeRoy Collins had the two-thirds majority to begin proceedings is disputed. Kennedy chose Johnson to attract Southern votes. Kennedy was a liberal Bostonian and Roman Catholic, while Johnson was more conservative, a Southerner, and a member of the Disciples of Christ. Labor leaders opposed Johnson, with AFL-CIO president George Meany calling him "the arch-foe of labor" and Illinois AFL-CIO president Reuben Soderstrom stating Kennedy had "made chumps out of leaders of the American labor movement." Johnson sought a third Senate term simultaneously with his vice presidential run. Robert Caro notes Johnson won both the vice presidency on the Kennedy–Johnson ticket and a third Senate term, having Texas law changed to allow him to run for both offices. Upon winning the vice presidency, he arranged to resign from the Senate as required by federal law when it convened on January 3, 1961. He won re-election with 1,306,605 votes (58 percent) to Republican John Tower’s 927,653 (41.1 percent). Fellow Democrat William A. Blakley was appointed to replace Johnson but lost a special election in May 1961 to Tower. After the election, Johnson sought authority not granted to vice presidents, initially requesting transfer of Senate majority leader powers, but faced opposition from the Democratic Caucus. He drafted an executive order for Kennedy’s signature granting him "general supervision" over national security and requiring government agencies to cooperate fully, but Kennedy responded with a non-binding letter requesting only a "review" of national security policies. Kennedy also declined early requests for Johnson to have an office adjacent to the Oval Office or a full-time staff. In 1961, Kennedy appointed Johnson’s friend Sarah T. Hughes to a federal judgeship. Johnson tried but failed to have Hughes nominated at the start of his vice presidency; House Speaker Sam Rayburn secured the appointment in exchange for support of an administration bill. Other White House members, including President Kennedy’s brother Robert F. Kennedy, openly despised Johnson and ridiculed his brusque manner. Congressman Tip O'Neill recalled the Kennedy staff "had a disdain for Johnson that they didn’t even try to hide" and took pride in snubbing him. Kennedy kept Johnson busy and informed, telling aides, "I can’t afford to have my vice president, who knows every reporter in Washington, going around saying we're all screwed up, so we're going to keep him happy." Kennedy appointed Johnson head of the President's Committee on Equal Employment Opportunities, where Johnson worked with African Americans and other minorities. Taylor Branch contends Johnson pushed the administration’s civil rights actions further and faster than Kennedy intended. Johnson undertook multiple minor diplomatic missions, including a visit to West Berlin on August 19–20, 1961, to calm Berliners outraged by the Berlin Wall. He attended Cabinet and National Security Council meetings. Kennedy gave Johnson control over all presidential appointments involving Texas and appointed him chairman of the President's Ad Hoc Committee for Science. After the Soviets achieved the first crewed spaceflight in April 1961, Kennedy assigned Johnson to evaluate the U.S. space program and recommend a project to catch up or surpass the Soviets. Johnson recommended committing to land an American on the Moon in the 1960s. Kennedy prioritized the space program, with Johnson’s appointment providing cover in case of failure. In August 1963, Johnson faced a Senate scandal when Bobby Baker, a protégé and secretary to Majority Leader, was investigated for alleged bribery and financial malfeasance. One witness claimed Baker arranged kickbacks for the Vice President. Baker resigned in October, and the investigation did not extend to Johnson. The negative publicity fueled rumors that Kennedy planned to drop Johnson from the 1964 ticket. However, on October 31, 1963, a reporter asked if Johnson would be retained, and Kennedy replied, "Yes to both those questions." There is little doubt Robert Kennedy and Johnson hated each other, yet both agreed dropping Johnson would cause heavy losses in the South. President Kennedy was assassinated on November 22, 1963, in Dallas, Texas. Later that day, Johnson took the presidential oath of office aboard Air Force One. Cecil Stoughton’s iconic photograph of Johnson taking the oath, with Mrs. Kennedy looking on, is the most famous photo ever taken aboard a presidential aircraft. Johnson was sworn in by District Court judge Sarah T. Hughes, making him the only U.S. president to be sworn in by a woman. Johnson believed it was essential to show immediate transition of power after the assassination to provide stability. He and the Secret Service, uncertain whether the assassin acted alone or as part of a conspiracy, felt compelled to return quickly to Washington, D.C., a move some criticized as too hasty. In response to public demand for answers and growing conspiracy theories, Johnson established the Warren Commission, headed by Chief Justice Earl Warren, to investigate Kennedy’s assassination. The commission concluded unanimously that Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone. Although Johnson publicly supported the findings, privately he expressed skepticism, telling advisor W. Marvin Watson in 1967 that he believed the CIA was involved, and shortly before his death, he told speechwriter Leo Janos, "I never believed that Oswald acted alone, although I can accept that he pulled the trigger." Upon assuming office, Johnson asked the existing Cabinet to remain in place. Despite his poor relationship with Johnson, Robert F. Kennedy stayed as Attorney General until September 1964, when he resigned to run for the U.S. Senate. Four Kennedy cabinet members—Dean Rusk, Stewart Udall, Orville L. Freeman, and W. Willard Wirtz—served until the end of Johnson’s presidency. Other holdovers, including Robert McNamara, left during Johnson’s tenure. Johnson had no official chief of staff; Walter Jenkins managed daily operations, and George Reedy became press secretary in March 1964 after Pierre Salinger left. Horace Busby served primarily as a speechwriter and political analyst, and Bill Moyers handled scheduling and speechwriting part-time. Johnson sought to quickly pursue Kennedy’s goal of a tax cut. He negotiated with Senator Harry F. Byrd of Virginia to reduce the budget below $100 billion in exchange for overwhelming Senate approval of the Revenue Act of 1964. The act cut individual income tax rates by about 20 percent, reduced the top marginal rate from 91 to 70 percent, and slightly lowered corporate tax rates. Passage of the tax cut helped advance civil rights legislation. Despite strong economic growth, heavy spending on the Vietnam War and domestic programs led to a rising budget deficit and inflation into the 1970s. To counter this, Johnson reluctantly signed the Revenue and Expenditure Control Act of 1968, which included tax increases and spending cuts, producing a budget surplus. On November 27, 1963, Johnson delivered his "Let Us Continue" speech to Congress, stating, "No memorial oration or eulogy could more eloquently honor President Kennedy's memory than the earliest possible passage of the Civil Rights Bill for which he fought so long." The national grief following the assassination gave strong momentum to Johnson’s promise to fulfill Kennedy’s civil rights agenda. Johnson asked Robert Kennedy to lead the effort on Capitol Hill, providing political cover if it failed and ensuring Johnson would receive credit if successful. Biographer Caro notes the bill Kennedy submitted faced tactics used to block past civil rights legislation, including Southern obstruction of urgent bills, especially the tax reform bill. To get the bill to the House floor, Johnson used a discharge petition to force it onto the floor. Facing pressure, the House Rules Committee approved the bill and moved it to the full House, which passed it 290–110. Johnson convinced Senate Majority Leader Mike Mansfield to send the House bill directly to the full Senate, bypassing the Senate Judiciary Committee and its segregationist chairman James Eastland. With committee bottlenecks no longer viable, anti-civil rights senators resorted to the filibuster, requiring at least 20 Republican votes. As Republicans grew less supportive due to their presidential nominee opposing the bill, the filibuster was overcome. According to Caro, the bill passed.

Robert F. Kennedy was considered an ideal choice for Johnson's vice presidential running mate, but Johnson and Kennedy had a poor relationship, and Johnson feared Kennedy would be credited with his election, so he consistently opposed the idea. Kennedy was hesitant to accept the offer, knowing it would upset Johnson. Barry Goldwater’s declining polling numbers reduced the political importance of selecting a running mate, making Hubert Humphrey’s selection a foregone conclusion and strengthening Johnson in the Midwest and industrial Northeast. To ensure loyalty, Johnson subjected Humphrey to a series of interviews and kept the announcement from the press until the last moment to maximize media speculation. In preparation for the 1964 Democratic convention in Atlantic City, Johnson requested 30 FBI agents to monitor convention activities, focusing particularly on the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party (MFDP) delegation, which sought to replace the white segregationist delegation. The FBI conducted wiretaps on Martin Luther King Jr., the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC), and the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE), all framed as monitoring disruptive activities that could endanger the president. Johnson was deeply concerned about media coverage of the credentials fight between the MFDP and the segregationist delegation and assigned Humphrey to manage the situation. The Credentials Committee seated two MFDP delegates as observers and agreed to bar future delegations from states where citizens were denied the right to vote due to race or color, but the MFDP rejected the ruling. The convention was seen as a personal triumph for Johnson, though the marginalization of the MFDP caused disaffection among the left and was later called a "turning point in the civil rights movement" by SNCC chairman John Lewis. Early in the 1964 campaign, Barry Goldwater appeared strong, especially in the South, threatening Johnson’s position, but Goldwater lost momentum. On September 7, 1964, Johnson’s campaign aired the "Daisy ad," showing a girl picking petals from a daisy followed by a nuclear explosion, implying that voting for Goldwater could lead to nuclear war. Goldwater’s campaign was symbolized by the bumper sticker "In your heart, you know he's right," while Johnson’s opponents used "In your heart, you know he might" and "In your guts, you know he's nuts." CIA Director William Colby claimed Tracy Barnes directed the CIA to spy on the Goldwater campaign and Republican National Committee to provide information to Johnson’s team. Johnson won the presidency by a landslide with 61.05 percent of the popular vote, the highest ever, and the largest margin in the 20th century—over 15.95 million votes—later surpassed by Nixon in 1972. In the Electoral College, Johnson defeated Goldwater 486 to 52, winning 44 states compared to Goldwater’s six, and secured a Senate majority of 68–32 and a House majority of 295–140, the largest majorities since FDR’s 1936 election. After the murder of civil rights worker Viola Liuzzo, Johnson announced the arrest of four Ku Klux Klan members involved in her death, denouncing the Klan as a "hooded society of bigots" and warning them to "return to a decent society before it's too late," becoming the first president since Ulysses S. Grant to do so. He promoted Christian redemption to gain support for civil rights, notably in his Howard University commencement address on June 4, 1965, where he stated that both government and nation must work to dismantle racial barriers and dissolve "antique enmities of the heart" that divide democracy and do great wrong to children of God. The Fair Housing Act, part of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, outlawed housing discrimination and enabled many African Americans to move to the suburbs. In April 1966, Johnson submitted a bill to Congress banning homeowners from refusing to enter into agreements based on race, which drew opposition from many Northerners who had supported prior civil rights legislation; although the bill passed the House, it failed in the Senate, marking Johnson’s first major legislative defeat. The bill gained momentum after Martin Luther King Jr.’s assassination on April 4, 1968, and the resulting civil unrest, and passed Congress on April 10, being signed into law by Johnson. In his 1964 State of the Union Address, Johnson declared an unconditional war on poverty, aiming not only to relieve but to cure and prevent it, and during his administration, the percentage of Americans living below the poverty line dropped from 23 to 12 percent. In August 1964, Johnson signed the Economic Opportunity Act of 1964, creating the Office of Economic Opportunity (OEO) to oversee local Community Action Agencies (CAA) that provided aid to the poor and required "maximum feasible participation" from local residents in designing and operating anti-poverty programs. This threatened local political leaders who viewed CAAs as alternative power structures, and in 1967, the Green Amendment gave city governments the right to decide which entity would be the official CAA, effectively halting the citizen participation movement. The act established the Job Corps and Volunteers in Service to America (VISTA), a domestic version of the Peace Corps; Job Corps provided academic and vocational training to low-income at-risk youth, modeled after the Civilian Conservation Corps, while VISTA deployed volunteers on community projects to address illiteracy, inadequate housing, and poor health, with 2,000 volunteers signing on by the end of 1965. Congress also approved Upward Bound, a program training low-income students for college. The act reflected Johnson’s belief that government could best assist the poor by providing economic opportunities. Johnson also convinced Congress to approve the Food Stamp Act of 1964, making permanent food stamp pilot programs initiated by President Kennedy. To combat homelessness, Johnson signed the Housing and Urban Development Act of 1965, providing rent subsidies for the elderly and disabled, funding the construction of 240,000 housing units, and allocating $3 billion for urban renewal. In September 1965, he signed legislation establishing the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to oversee these programs. The Appalachian Regional Development Act provided an additional $1.1 billion for roads, health clinics, and public works to improve living standards in Appalachia. Johnson launched the "Demonstration Cities Program" in 1964 to combat urban blight, requiring cities to demonstrate readiness to make substantial improvements, with a requested annual investment of $400 million totaling $2.4 billion; Congress passed a reduced version in late 1966, costing $900 million, which Johnson later called the Model Cities Program. The New York Times later described the program as largely a failure. Johnson’s initial healthcare effort was the creation of the Commission on Heart Disease, Cancer, and Strokes (HDCS), which accounted for 71 percent of U.S. deaths in 1962. In 1965, Johnson focused on hospital insurance for the elderly under Social Security, with Representative Wilbur Mills, Chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, playing a key role. To reduce Republican opposition, Mills proposed a three-tiered Medicare plan: hospital insurance under Social Security, a voluntary doctor visit insurance program, and an expanded medical welfare program for the poor administered through states as Medicaid. The bill passed the House by 110 votes on April 8 and the Senate on July 28, and Medicare now covers tens of millions of Americans. The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 reformed the immigration system by repealing the National Origins Formula, which had restricted immigration from outside Western Europe and the Western Hemisphere; the annual immigration rate doubled between 1965 and 1970 and doubled again by 1990, with significant increases from Asia and Latin America, including Mexico. Scholars give Johnson little credit for the law, which was not a priority, as he had previously supported the unpopular McCarren–Walter Act of 1952. Johnson, who had overcome poverty through public education in Texas, believed education was essential to the American dream, especially for minorities, and made it a top priority of the Great Society. After his 1964 landslide victory, in early 1965 he proposed the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (ESEA), which would double federal education spending from $4 billion to $8 billion, and the bill passed both houses by wide margins. ESEA increased funding to all school districts but directed more funds to those with large proportions of poor students. Although ESEA strengthened Johnson’s support among K–12 teachers’ unions, neither the Higher Education Act nor new endowments eased growing unease among college professors and students over the Vietnam War. Johnson’s second major education program was the Higher Education Act of 1965, which increased federal funding to universities, created scholarships, provided low-interest student loans, and established a Teacher Corps. He also established Head Start, an early education program for disadvantaged children, and in 1967 signed the Public Broadcasting Act to create educational television programs. In 1965, Johnson created the National Endowment for the Humanities and the National Endowment for the Arts to support the study of literature, history, law, and the arts such as music, painting, and sculpture. In March 1966, Johnson sent a transportation message proposing the creation of a new Transportation Department, comprising the Commerce Department’s Office of Transportation, the Bureau of Public Roads, the Federal Aviation Agency, the Coast Guard, the Maritime Administration, the Civil Aeronautics Board, and the Interstate Commerce Commission. The bill passed the Senate after negotiations over navigation projects and the House.

Students grew increasingly uneasy with the war in Vietnam. Johnson's second major education initiative was the Higher Education Act of 1965, which increased federal funding to universities, created scholarships, provided low-interest loans to students, and established a Teacher Corps. Johnson also launched Head Start, an early education program to assist children from disadvantaged families in preparing for success in public schools. In 1967, he signed the Public Broadcasting Act to create educational television programs to supplement broadcast networks. In 1965, Johnson established the National Endowment for the Humanities and the National Endowment for the Arts to support the study of literature, history, and law, and the arts such as music, painting, and sculpture. In March 1966, Johnson sent a transportation message to Congress proposing a new Transportation Department composed of the Commerce Department's Office of Transportation, the Bureau of Public Roads, the Federal Aviation Agency, the Coast Guard, the Maritime Administration, the Civil Aeronautics Board, and the Interstate Commerce Commission. The bill passed the Senate after negotiation over navigation projects; in the House, passage required negotiation over maritime interests, and it was signed on October 15, 1965. During his presidency, Johnson signed over 300 conservation measures, forming the legal foundation of the modern environmental movement. He signed the Clean Air Act of 1963, proposed by President Kennedy, which set emission standards for stationary air pollutant sources and directed federal funding for air quality research. In 1965, the act was amended by the Motor Vehicle Air Pollution Control Act, which required the federal government to establish and enforce national standards for controlling pollutants from new motor vehicles and engines. In September 1964, Johnson signed the Wilderness Act, creating the National Wilderness Preservation System that preserved 9.1 million acres of forestland from industrial development, and signed a law establishing the Land and Water Conservation Fund to aid in the purchase of land for federal and state parks. In 1965, First Lady Lady Bird Johnson led efforts to pass the Highway Beautification Act, which required control of outdoor advertising, including removal of certain signs, along the nation's Interstate Highway System and federal-aid primary highways, mandated removal or screening of junkyards along these roads, and encouraged scenic enhancement and roadside development. Though Johnson introduced a gun control bill on June 6, 1968, after Robert Kennedy's assassination, Lady Bird Johnson's press secretary Liz Carpenter warned that the country had been "brainwashed by high drama" and that Johnson "needed some quick dramatic actions" to address violence. In October 1968, Johnson signed the Gun Control Act, which prohibited convicted felons, drug users, and the mentally ill from purchasing handguns, raised record-keeping and licensing requirements, and banned mail order sales of rifles and shotguns. The nation experienced a series of "long hot summers" of civil unrest during Johnson's presidency, beginning with the Harlem riots in 1964 and the Watts district of Los Angeles in 1965. The momentum for civil rights stalled after the Watts riots, when 34 people were killed and $35 million (equivalent to $349.22 million in 2024) in property was damaged, leading to fears of nationwide violence and a loss of appetite for additional programs in Johnson's agenda. In what is known as the "Long Hot Summer of 1967," more than 150 riots erupted across the United States. The Boston Globe described it as "a revolution of black Americans against white Americans, a violent petition for the redress of long-standing grievances." The Newark riots resulted in 26 deaths and 1,500 injuries; the Detroit riot caused 43 deaths, 2,250 injuries, 4,000 arrests, and millions of dollars in property damage. Governor George Romney deployed 7,400 National Guard troops to stop fire bombings, looting, and attacks on businesses and police. Johnson eventually sent federal troops with tanks and machine guns. At an August 2, 1967, cabinet meeting, Attorney General Ramsey Clark warned that untrained and undisciplined local police and National Guardsmen might trigger a "guerrilla war in the streets," as evidenced by sniper fire in Newark and Detroit, with shooters often targeting from rooftops and concealed locations. Johnson's popularity declined as a massive white political backlash emerged, reinforcing the perception that he had lost control of major cities and his own party. To investigate the causes of urban civil disorder, Johnson created the 11-member Kerner Commission, headed by Illinois Governor Otto Kerner. The commission's 1968 report recommended legislative measures to promote racial integration and alleviate poverty and concluded that the nation was "moving toward two societies, one black, one white—separate and unequal." According to Press Secretary George Christian, Johnson was unsurprised by the riots, saying: "What did you expect? ... When you put your foot on a man's neck and hold him down for three hundred years, and then you let him up, what's he going to do? He's going to knock your block off." In 1966, the press identified a credibility gap between what Johnson said in press conferences and what was happening in the Vietnam War, leading to less favorable coverage. By the end of 1966, Democratic Governor Warren E. Hearnes of Missouri warned that Johnson would lose the state by 100,000 votes, despite winning by 500,000 in 1964. "Frustration over Vietnam; too much federal spending and ... taxation; no great public support for your Great Society programs; and ... public disenchantment with the civil rights programs" had eroded the president's standing. There were bright spots; in January 1967, Johnson claimed wages were the highest in history, unemployment was at a 13-year low, and corporate profits and farm incomes were greater than ever; a 4.5 percent increase in consumer prices and rising interest rates were concerns. Johnson requested a temporary 6 percent income tax surcharge to cover the growing deficit. His approval ratings remained below 50 percent, and in December 1966, his disapproval rating exceeded his approval rating. In January 1967, the number of his strong supporters dropped to 16 percent, from 25 percent four months earlier. When asked to explain his declining popularity, Johnson said, "I am a dominating personality, and when I get things done I don't always please all the people." He also blamed the press, claiming they showed "complete irresponsibility and lie and misstate facts and have no one to be answerable to," and "the preachers, liberals and professors" who had turned against him. In the 1966 congressional elections, Republicans gained three Senate seats and 47 House seats, reinvigorating the conservative coalition and making it harder for Johnson to pass additional Great Society legislation. However, Congress ultimately passed nearly 96 percent of the administration's Great Society programs. During the Johnson administration, NASA conducted the Gemini crewed space program, developed the Saturn V rocket and its launch facility, and prepared for the first crewed Apollo missions. On January 27, 1967, the entire Apollo 1 crew was killed in a cabin fire during a spacecraft test on the launch pad, halting the Apollo program. Rather than appointing a Warren-style commission, Johnson accepted Administrator James E. Webb's request for NASA to conduct its own investigation. Johnson maintained strong support for Apollo despite congressional and press controversy, and the program recovered. The first two crewed missions, Apollo 7 and the first crewed flight to the Moon, Apollo 8, were completed by the end of his term. He congratulated the Apollo 8 crew, saying, "You've taken ... all of us, all over the world, into a new era." On July 16, 1969, Johnson attended the launch of the Apollo 11 mission, becoming the first former or incumbent U.S. president to witness a rocket launch. The Vietnam War began in 1955 when Communist forces started operating in South Vietnam. By the time Johnson took office, there were 16,700 American military personnel in South Vietnam. Despite some misgivings, Johnson ultimately supported escalation of the U.S. role in Vietnam. Like most American leaders in the mid-1960s, he was committed to preventing the spread of Communism. His decision to escalate was also influenced by reputation; under pressure from pro-war politicians like Barry Goldwater, Johnson feared that failing to stand firm in Vietnam would damage his domestic political credibility and the international reputation of the United States. On October 11, 1963, President Kennedy signed NSAM 263, ordering the withdrawal of 1,000 military personnel by the end of the year following the McNamara–Taylor mission report. On November 26, Johnson signed NSAM 273, reaffirming the Kennedy administration's withdrawal approval and continuing support for South Vietnam. In August 1964, ambiguous evidence suggested two U.S. destroyers were attacked by North Vietnamese torpedo boats in international waters in the Gulf of Tonkin. Although Johnson wanted to avoid discussing Vietnam in the 1964 election campaign, he felt compelled to respond to the alleged Communist aggression. He obtained from Congress the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution on August 7, 1964, granting blanket congressional approval for the use of military force to repel future attacks. Johnson decided on a systematic bombing campaign, known as Operation Rolling Thunder, in February 1965 after a Viet Cong attack on Pleiku Air Base killed eight Americans. The U.S. continued bombing North Vietnam until late 1968. In March 1965, McGeorge Bundy called for American ground operations; Johnson agreed and quietly changed the mission from defensive to offensive operations. On March 8, 1965, 3,500 troops landed near Da Nang, the first time U.S. combat forces had been sent to mainland Asia since the Korean War. In June, South Vietnamese Ambassador Maxwell D. Taylor reported that the bombing offensive against North Vietnam had been ineffective and that the South Vietnamese army was outclassed and in danger of collapse. In late July, McNamara and Johnson's top advisors recommended increasing U.S. soldiers from 75,000 to over 200,000. Johnson agreed but felt constrained by unpalatable choices: sending more troops would make him appear interventionist, and not sending more would risk impeachment. By October 1965, over 200,000 troops were deployed in Vietnam. Throughout 1965, few members of Congress or the administration openly criticized Johnson's handling of the war. In early 1966, Senator Robert F. Kennedy sharply criticized Johnson's bombing campaign, stating the U.S. may be headed "on a road from which there is no turning back, a road that leads to catastrophe for all mankind." Soon after, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, chaired by Senator James William Fulbright, held televised hearings on the administration's Vietnam policy. In July, polling showed Americans favored the bombing campaign by a five-to-one margin; however, in August a Defense Department study found the bombing had minimal impact on North Vietnam. By late 1966, multiple sources reported progress was being made against North Vietnamese logistics and infrastructure, and Johnson was urged to begin peace discussions. English philosopher Bertrand Russell initiated the International War Crimes Tribunal to condemn the American effort. The gap with Hanoi, however, remained an unbridgeable demand for a unilateral end to bombing and withdrawal of forces. Johnson grew increasingly anxious about justifying war casualties and spoke of the need for decisive victory, despite the war's unpopularity. By the end of 1966, it was clear that the air campaign and pacification efforts had failed, and Johnson agreed to McNamara's recommendation to add 70,000 troops in 1967 and the CIA's recommendation to increase bombings against North Vietnam. The bombing escalation ended secret talks with North Vietnam, but U.S. leaders did not consider North Vietnamese intentions in those talks to be genuine. By mid-1967, nearly 70,000 Americans had been killed or wounded in the war, which was commonly described as a "stalemate." In January and February, probes were made to assess North Vietnam's willingness to discuss peace, but they were ignored. Ho Chi Minh declared that the only solution was a unilateral U.S. withdrawal. A Gallup, Inc. poll in July 1967 showed that 52 percent of Americans disapproved of Johnson's handling of the war, and only 34 percent believed progress was being made. Nonetheless, Johnson agreed to an increase of 55,000 troops, bringing the total to 525,000. In August, Johnson, with the Joint Chiefs' support, expanded the air campaign and exempted only Hanoi, Haiphong, and a buffer zone with China from the target list. Later that month, McNamara told a Senate subcommittee that an expanded air campaign would not bring Hanoi to the peace table. The Joint Chiefs were stunned and threatened mass resignation; McNamara was summoned to the White House for a three-hour dressing down. Nevertheless, Johnson had received CIA reports confirming McNamara's analysis at least in part. In the meantime, an election establishing a constitutional government in the South concluded and provided hope for peace talks. With the war in a stalemate and widespread disapproval of the conflict, Johnson convened a group of veteran government foreign policy experts, informally known as "the Wise Men": Dean Acheson, General Omar Bradley, George Ball, McGeorge Bundy, Arthur Dean, C. Douglas Dillon, Abe Fortas, Averell Harriman, Henry Cabot Lodge, Robert Daniel Murphy, and Maxwell D. Taylor. They unanimously opposed leaving Vietnam and encouraged Johnson to "stay the course." Afterward, on November 17, in a nationally televised address, Johnson assured the public, "We are inflicting greater losses than we're taking...We are making progress." Less than two weeks later, Robert McNamara announced his resignation as Defense Secretary. Behind closed doors, he had regularly expressed doubts about Johnson's war strategy, angering the president. He joined a growing list of Johnson's top aides who resigned over the war, including Bill Moyers, McGeorge Bundy, and George Ball. In October, with increasing public protests against the war, Johnson engaged the FBI and the CIA to investigate, monitor, and undermine anti-war activists. In mid-October, a demonstration of 100,000 people gathered at the Pentagon; Johnson and Dean Rusk believed foreign communist sources were behind the demonstration, but the CIA's findings refuted that. On January 30, 1968, the Viet Cong and the North Vietnamese Army launched the Tet Offensive against South Vietnam's five largest cities, including Saigon. Although the offensive failed militarily, it was a psychological victory that definitively turned American public opinion against the war effort. In February 1968, influential news anchor Walter Cronkite of CBS News stated on air that the conflict was deadlocked and that further fighting would change nothing. Johnson responded, saying, "If I've lost Cronkite, I've lost middle America." Demoralization about the war was widespread; 26 percent approved of Johnson's handling of Vietnam, while 63 percent disapproved. College students and others protested, burned draft cards, and chanted, "Hey, hey, LBJ, how many kids did you kill today?" The Tet Offensive convinced senior leaders of the Johnson administration, including the "Wise Men" and new Defense Secretary Clark Clifford, that further escalation of troop levels would not end the war. Johnson was initially reluctant to follow this advice but ultimately agreed to allow a partial bombing halt and to signal his willingness to engage in peace talks. On March 31, 1968, Johnson announced he would halt the bombing in North Vietnam while also announcing that he would not seek re-election. He also escalated U.S. military operations in South Vietnam to maintain pressure.

Influential CBS News anchor Walter Cronkite stated on air that the Vietnam conflict was deadlocked and that further fighting would not alter the outcome, prompting President Lyndon B. Johnson to remark, "If I've lost Cronkite, I've lost middle America." By this time, public disapproval of Johnson's Vietnam policy was widespread: 26 percent approved of his handling of the war, while 63 percent disapproved. College students and others protested, burned draft cards, and chanted, "Hey, hey, LBJ, how many kids did you kill today?" The Tet Offensive led senior Johnson administration figures, including the "Wise Men" and new Defense Secretary Clark Clifford, to conclude that increasing troop levels would not end the war. Though initially reluctant, Johnson eventually agreed to a partial bombing halt and signaled willingness to engage in peace talks. On March 31, 1968, he announced a halt to bombing in North Vietnam and declared he would not seek re-election. At the same time, he escalated U.S. military operations in South Vietnam to consolidate control before serious peace talks began in Paris in May, though those talks failed to produce results. Major obstacles included the U.S. refusal to allow the Viet Cong in the South Vietnamese government and North Vietnam's refusal to recognize South Vietnam's legitimacy. In October 1968, when a bombing halt agreement was nearly reached, Republican nominee Richard Nixon intervened with South Vietnam, promising better terms to delay settlement until after the election. Johnson sought to continue talks after the 1968 election, but North Vietnam delayed negotiations until after Nixon took office. Like President Kennedy, Johnson sought to isolate Cuba, which was ruled by Soviet-aligned Fidel Castro. In 1965, the Dominican Civil War erupted between President Donald Reid Cabral's government and supporters of former president Juan Bosch. On advice from Abe Fortas, Johnson sent over 20,000 Marines to the Dominican Republic to evacuate American citizens and restore order, helping arrange new elections. This use of force alienated many in Latin America, reducing the region's importance in Johnson's foreign policy, which became increasingly focused on Vietnam. Despite active engagement in Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Latin America, Johnson prioritized arms control with the Soviet Union. The USSR sought closer ties during the mid-to-late 1960s due to the worsening Sino-Soviet split. Johnson attempted to ease trade restrictions with China, but the start of China's Cultural Revolution ended hopes of rapprochement. Concerned about nuclear war, Johnson pursued arms control, signing the Outer Space Treaty and the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, and laid the groundwork for Strategic Arms Limitation Talks. He held a friendly meeting with Soviet Premier Alexei Kosygin at the 1967 Glassboro Summit Conference and, in July 1968, the U.S., Britain, and the Soviet Union signed the Non-Proliferation Treaty, agreeing not to assist other nations in developing nuclear weapons. A planned U.S.-Soviet nuclear disarmament summit was canceled after Soviet forces violently suppressed the Prague Spring. Johnson continued the FBI's wiretapping of Martin Luther King Jr., authorized by the Kennedy administration under Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy, and also authorized tapping phone conversations of others, including Vietnamese friends of a Nixon associate. Johnson made eleven international trips to twenty countries during his presidency, flying 523,000 miles (841,690 km) on Air Force One. His October 1966 visit to Australia sparked anti-war demonstrations. In a unique trip before Christmas 1967, Johnson began by visiting the memorial for Australian Prime Minister Harold Holt, presumed drowned in a swimming accident; the White House did not inform the press in advance. The trip, covering 26,959 miles (43,386.3 km), took only 112.5 hours (4.7 days), with Air Force One crossing the equator twice, stopping at Travis Air Force Base, Honolulu, Pago Pago, Canberra, Melbourne, Vietnam, Karachi, and Rome. Though having served less than two years of Kennedy's term, Johnson was constitutionally eligible for a second full term in 1968. Despite declining popularity, conventional wisdom believed a sitting president could not be denied re-nomination. In September 1967, Johnson openly admitted he was considering dropping out. He won a narrow victory in the New Hampshire primary on March 12, but on March 31, in a speech, announced he would not seek or accept the party nomination, shocking the nation. The next day, his approval ratings rose from 36 percent to 49 percent. Historians have debated his decision: Shesol says he wanted to leave and sought vindication; Woods says he realized the nation needed healing; Dallek says he had no further domestic goals, his popularity had eroded, his health was poor, and his wife urged retirement; Bennett argues he was forced out due to outrage over Vietnam policy. Johnson may have hoped the convention would later draft him back. Vice President Hubert Humphrey entered the race after Johnson's withdrawal, making the 1968 Democratic primaries a three-way contest between Humphrey, Robert F. Kennedy, and George McGovern. Kennedy won support from the poor and working class and gained ground in primaries, but was assassinated in June by Sirhan Sirhan. With Johnson's support, Humphrey won the nomination at the tumultuous 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, where violent police attacks on anti-war protesters occurred. Humphrey's polling improved after a September 30 speech in which he broke with Johnson's war policy, calling for an end to bombing North Vietnam. On October 31, 1968, Johnson announced to the nation that he had ordered a complete cessation of all air, naval, and artillery bombardment of North Vietnam, effective November 1, if the North Vietnamese government was willing to negotiate, citing progress in Paris talks. Republican nominee Richard Nixon won the election. Johnson appointed Justices Abe Fortas (1965) and Thurgood Marshall (1967) to the Supreme Court. Anticipating court challenges to his 1965 legislation, Johnson believed having a "mole" in the Court would provide inside information. He pushed for Fortas to take Arthur Goldberg's UN ambassador seat, despite Fortas's wife objecting due to his early career. When Earl Warren retired in 1968, Johnson nominated Fortas for Chief Justice and Homer Thornberry for associate justice, but both nominations were filibustered and never voted on by the full Senate. On Inauguration Day (January 20, 1969), Johnson saw Nixon sworn in, then flew back to Texas. When the plane's front door closed, he pulled out a cigarette—his first since his 1955 heart attack—his daughter pulled it out and said, "Daddy, what are you doing? You're going to kill yourself." He returned and said, "I've now raised you, girls. I've now been President. Now it's my time!" From then on, he entered a self-destructive spiral. After leaving office, Johnson returned to his ranch in Stonewall, Texas, with former aide Harry J. Middleton, who drafted his first book, The Choices We Face, and worked on his memoirs, The Vantage Point: Perspectives of the Presidency 1963–1969, published in 1971. The Lyndon Baines Johnson Library and Museum opened on the UT Austin campus in 1971. He donated his Texas ranch to the public to form the Lyndon B. Johnson National Historical Park, with the condition that it remain a working ranch, not a sterile relic. Johnson gave Nixon high grades in foreign policy but worried that his successor would pressure U.S. forces out of South Vietnam before the South Vietnamese could defend themselves, warning, "If the South falls to the Communists, we can have a serious backlash here at home." During the 1972 presidential election, Johnson reluctantly endorsed Democratic nominee George McGovern, a senator from South Dakota who opposed Johnson's foreign and defense policies. Johnson wanted to attend the Democratic National Convention but was advised against it due to lack of welcome. He was dismayed by McGovern's nomination and platform, insisting that "if only the Democrats don't go too far left, Nixon could be defeated," and believing Edmund Muskie would be more likely to defeat Nixon, though he declined to intervene, fearing his unpopularity would help McGovern. Johnson's protégé John Connally, who had served as Nixon's Secretary of the Treasury and later headed "Democrats for Nixon," became Johnson's political opponent in the general election. Johnson married Claudia Alta "Lady Bird" Taylor from Karnack, Texas, after meeting at Georgetown University Law Center. During their first date, he asked her to marry him; after many dates, she agreed. The wedding was officiated by Arthur R. McKinstry at St. Mark's Episcopal Church in San Antonio. They had two daughters: Lynda Bird in 1944 and Luci Baines in 1947. Johnson gave his children names with the LBJ initials; his dog was named Little Beagle Johnson, and his home was the LBJ Ranch in the Texas Hill Country. His initials appeared on cufflinks, ashtrays, and clothes. During his marriage, Johnson had affairs with "numerous" women, including socialite Alice Marsh, considered his most important relationship outside marriage. On July 2, 1955, at age 46, Johnson, a 60-cigarette-per-day smoker, suffered a near-fatal heart attack, leading him to quit smoking. Five months later, doctors reported a "most satisfactory recovery." Johnson may have suffered a second heart attack after Kennedy's assassination, though publicly diagnosed with an angina attack. On November 8, 1965, he underwent surgery at Bethesda Naval Hospital to remove his gallbladder and a kidney stone; doctors reported he had come through the surgery "beautifully as expected," and he resumed duties the next day, meeting with reporters to reassure the public. Although incapacitated during surgery, no presidential power was transferred to Vice President Humphrey. In March 1970, Johnson suffered an angina attack and was taken to Brooke Army General Hospital in San Antonio. He had gained over 25 pounds (11 kg) since leaving office, weighing around 235 pounds (107 kg), and was urged to lose weight. By summer 1970, gripped by chronic chest pains, he lost 15 pounds (6.8 kg) in less than a month on a crash water diet. He resumed smoking shortly before Christmas 1971, after not smoking since his 1955 heart attack. In April 1972, Johnson had another major heart attack while visiting his daughter Lynda in Virginia, confiding to friends, "I'm hurting real bad." Chest pains returned nearly every afternoon, leaving him frightened and breathless. A portable oxygen tank was kept by his bed, and he frequently lay down to use it. He continued to smoke heavily and, though nominally on a low-calorie, low-cholesterol diet, adhered to it only intermittently. He also began experiencing severe abdominal pains, diagnosed as diverticulosis. His heart condition worsened rapidly, and surgery was recommended. Johnson flew to Houston to consult with heart specialist Michael DeBakey, who found that despite two coronary arteries needing bypass, his heart was in such poor condition that he likely would have died during surgery. On January 12, 1973, Johnson recorded an hour-long television interview with Walter Cronkite at his ranch, discussing his legacy, especially the civil rights movement. He was still smoking heavily and told Cronkite it was better for his heart "to smoke than to be nervous." At approximately 3:50 P.M. Central on January 22, 1973, Johnson suffered his final heart attack in his bedroom. He managed to telephone Secret Service agents, who found him unconscious and "appearing to be dead," holding the receiver. They attempted resuscitation and airlifted him to San Antonio International Airport, where cardiologist George McGranahan pronounced him dead on arrival at 4:33 P.M. Johnson was 64. Shortly after his death, press secretary Tom Johnson (no relation) called Cronkite to inform him, who was anchoring CBS Evening News live and reported the news directly. Nixon mentioned Johnson's death in a speech the day after, announcing the peace agreement to end the Vietnam War. Johnson was honored with a state funeral. His body lay in repose at the LBJ Presidential Library in Austin before being flown to Washington, D.C., where it lay in state at the U.S. Capitol, with eulogies delivered by J. J. Pickle and Dean Rusk. The state funeral service took place on January 25, 1973, at the National City Christian Church in Washington, D.C., where Johnson had worshipped during his presidency. The service was presided over by President Nixon and attended by foreign dignitaries, including Japanese Prime Minister Eisaku Satō. Eulogies were delivered by George Davis, the church's pastor, and W. Marvin Watson, Johnson's last postmaster general and longtime adviser. Later that day, Johnson was buried in his family's private cemetery in Gillespie County, Texas, near his birthplace. Reverend Billy Graham officiated the burial, and former Texas governor John Connally delivered a eulogy; several hundred people attended. The state funeral—the last for a president until Richard Nixon's in 1994—occurred the same week as Nixon's second inauguration. Because Johnson died two days after the inauguration, some inauguration-related activities were canceled. The state funeral—the last for a president until Richard Nixon's in 1994—occurred the same week as Nixon's second inauguration. Because Johnson died two days after the inauguration, some inauguration-related activities were canceled. According to biographer Randall Woods, Johnson posed in many different roles: "Johnson the Son of the Tenant Farmer, Johnson the Great Compromiser, Johnson the All-Knowing, Johnson the Humble, Johnson the Warrior, Johnson the Dove, Johnson the Romantic, Johnson the Hard-Headed Pragmatist, Johnson the Preserver of Traditions, Johnson the Crusader for Social Justice, Johnson the Magnanimous, Johnson the Vindictive or Johnson the Uncouth, LBJ the Hick, Lyndon the Satyr, and Johnson the Usurper." Johnson had his particular brand of persuasion known as "The Johnson Treatment." "There was no more powerful majority leader in American history," biographer Robert Dallek writes. Dallek stated that Johnson had biographies on all the senators, knew what their ambitions, hopes, and tastes were, and used it to his advantage in securing votes. Another Johnson biographer noted, "He could get up every day and learn what their fears, their desires, their wishes, their wants were and he could then manipulate, dominate, persuade and cajole them." As president, Johnson vetoed 30 bills; no other president in history vetoed so many bills and never had a single one overridden by Congress. He was often seen as an ambitious, tireless, and imposing figure who was ruthlessly effective at getting legislation passed. He typically worked 18- to 20-hour days without a break and had no regular leisure activities. He stood 6 feet 3.5 inches (1.918 m) tall. Johnson's cowboy hat and boots reflected his Texas roots and love of the rural hill country. From 250 acres (100 ha) of land that he was given by an aunt in 1951, he created a 2,700-acre (1,100 ha) working ranch with 400 cattle. The National Park Service keeps a herd descended from Johnson's and maintains the ranch property. Biographer Randall Woods argues that Social Gospel themes Johnson learned from childhood allowed him to transform social problems into moral problems, which helps explain his longtime commitment to social justice and explicitly inspired his foreign-policy approach to Christian internationalism and nation-building. For example, in a 1966 speech he quoted at length from the Social Creed of the Methodist Church, adding "It would be very hard for me to write a more perfect description of the American ideal." Scholars have viewed Johnson through the lens of both his legislative achievements and his lack of success in the Vietnam War. His overall rating among historians has remained relatively steady, and his average ranking is higher than any of the eight presidents who followed him, although similar to Reagan and Clinton. In public polling of presidential favorability, Johnson tends to appear more toward the bottom of lists, typically excepting Donald Trump, George W. Bush, and Richard Nixon, and sometimes Gerald Ford. Historian Kent Germany explains: "The man who was elected to the White House by one of the widest margins in U.S. history and pushed through as much legislation as any other American politician now seems to be remembered best by the public for succeeding an assassinated hero, steering the country into a quagmire in Vietnam, cheating on his saintly wife, exposing his stitched-up belly, using profanity, picking up dogs by their ears, swimming naked with advisers in the White House pool, and emptying his bowels while conducting official business. Of all those issues, Johnson's reputation suffers the most from his management of the Vietnam War, something that has overshadowed his civil rights and domestic policy accomplishments and caused Johnson himself to regret his handling of 'the woman I really loved — the Great Society.'" The Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston was renamed the Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in 1973, and the United States Department of Education headquarters was named after Johnson in 2007. The Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs at the University of Texas at Austin was named in his honor, as is the Lyndon B. Johnson National Grassland. Also named for him are schools in Austin and Laredo, Texas; Melbourne, Florida; and Jackson, Kentucky. Interstate 635 in Dallas is named the Lyndon B. Johnson Freeway. The Lyndon Baines Johnson Memorial Grove on the Potomac was dedicated in 1976. Johnson was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously in 1980. Texas created a state holiday on August 27 to mark Johnson's birthday, known as Lyndon Baines Johnson Day.
